correctness.rationale: Exact companion-matrix trace and determinant plus the strict Jury criterion give the deterministic periodic interval and exclude marginal boundaries; an independently derived symmetric-covariance recurrence and positive Lyapunov form give the iid mean-square criterion for all deterministic starts. The necessary condition follows from the covariance eigenvalue at and above cutoff and spanning of deterministic rank-one covariance initial conditions. A strictly increasing crossover polynomial gives unique reversal, monotonicity of its roots, and the logarithmic asymptotic. The supplied local symbolic program checked the matrix identities and rational examples; finite checks are not used as infinite proofs.

originality.rationale: The iid frontier and elementary two-period Floquet stability calculations have direct published predecessors and are excluded from the novelty claim. The assessed claim is their exact matched-frequency contrast for every integer sampling period, the unique momentum reversal, and its strictly increasing logarithmic boundary-layer law. Actual searches and full primary theorem comparisons did not identify a dominating equivalence; switched-recursion literature leaves a real residual risk.
residual_risks: The scalar iid mean-square condition is previously known, and m=2 periodic algebra has strong prior overlap; neither component alone is novel.
An earlier generic switched linear system or control paper may contain the exact comparative root as a special case.

Comparison is of deterministic stability with iid mean-square stability, not matching almost-sure contraction metrics; performance significance is therefore limited to sharp admissible-step robustness.

value.rationale: At fixed average gradient-delivery frequency, selecting temporal correlation can reverse the maximum stable active-step strength exactly once as momentum changes. The closed all-period boundary, its strict monotonicity and logarithmic high-period layer provide a motivated design law for intermittent-gradient momentum. This is a stability-capacity result, not an optimal convergence-rate or cost theorem.
